intro: IRIG-B is the time code that substation relays have used for decades. A GPS clock sends one frame per second over a coax cable or a twisted pair of wires: 100 bits, each 10 ms long. The width of each pulse tells what it is: a 0, a 1 or a position marker. The first edge of the frame marks the exact start of the second.
plain: This time code works like the time signal on the radio: the start of each second is marked exactly, and a short code says what time it is. A clock that listens to satellites sends a pattern of short and long pulses down a wire, once a second. Every protection device on the wire reads the pattern and sets its own clock. When something goes wrong, they all write down the same time, so the order of events is clear.

lock.title: Lock to GPS
lock.text: The station clock hears the satellites through its antenna and locks to UTC (Coordinated Universal Time, the world's reference time). From now on it starts each IRIG-B frame exactly on the second.

frame.title: One frame
frame.text: At 10:41:07.000 a frame begins with two markers in a row. Then come the seconds, minutes, hours, day of year and year in BCD (binary-coded decimal: each decimal digit written in binary on its own). After them come the control bits, and the seconds of the day as one binary number. Every relay on the line hears the frame. IRIG-B has no addresses and no answers.

set.title: Set the clock
set.text: The time in a frame is the time of its first edge, but a relay only knows that time once it has read the whole frame. So the relay waits for the next frame, checks that it is exactly one second later, and sets its clock.

event.title: A breaker trips
event.text: A fault on feeder F1. Relay F1 trips breaker Q1, which opens, and stores the event with its own clock: 10:52:31.283. The records of every relay on this line share one time scale, so their order is clear.

holdover.title: Running without GPS
holdover.text: At 11:40 the antenna cable is cut. The clock runs on its own oscillator and keeps sending: this is called holdover. By 14:12 it estimates that its error may be up to 10 µs, and says so in the time quality bits: 5.

frames.f-hold: It is 14:12:31; my time may be 10 µs off

notes.gps: GPS radio signals, not IRIG-B. With four or more satellites in view, the clock knows UTC to well within a microsecond.
notes.trip: A copper wire to the breaker's trip coil, not IRIG-B. The event record is read later over the relay's data protocol, such as IEC 60870-5-103.
notes.lost: No IRIG-B here: the antenna cable is cut, and the clock no longer hears any satellite.

sec-07.name: Seconds
sec-07.note: 07 in BCD: the units digit 7 in bits 1–4, low bit first, then the tens digit 0 in bits 6–8. Shown here as hex, so it reads like the time.

sec-08.name: Seconds
sec-08.note: 08: one more than in the last frame.

sec-31.name: Seconds
sec-31.note: 31 in BCD: the units digit 1, then the tens digit 3.

min-41.name: Minutes
min-41.note: 41 in BCD: units in bits 10–13, tens in bits 15–17.

min-12.name: Minutes
min-12.note: 12 in BCD: the units digit 2, then the tens digit 1.

hour-10.name: Hours
hour-10.note: 10 in BCD: units in bits 20–23, tens in bits 25–26. UTC, as the offset bits say.

hour-14.name: Hours
hour-14.note: 14 in BCD: the units digit 4, then the tens digit 1.

day-316.name: Day of year
day-316.note: 316 = 12 November 2026, shown as 03 16. Units in bits 30–33, tens in 35–38, hundreds in 40–41.

year-26.name: Year
year-26.note: (20)26 in BCD, in bits 50–58. Codes without the year leave it to the relay.

cf-flags.name: Leap second · DST
cf-flags.note: Bits 60–63 (IEEE C37.118.1): no leap second pending, no daylight-saving change pending, no daylight saving time.

cf-offset.name: Time offset
cf-offset.note: Bits 64–68 and 70: 0 hours from UTC. This frame carries UTC.

tq-0.name: Time quality 0
tq-0.note: Bits 71–74: 0, locked to GPS, full accuracy.

tq-5.name: Time quality 5
tq-5.note: The clock's error may be up to 10 µs. 4 would mean 1 µs, 6 would mean 100 µs; 15 means the time is not reliable.

parity-0.name: Parity
parity-0.note: Bit 75: even parity. Bits 1–74 hold an even number of ones, so this bit is 0.

parity-1.name: Parity
parity-1.note: Bit 75: bits 1–74 hold 17 ones, so this bit is 1 and the count is even again.

sbs-38467.name: Straight binary seconds
sbs-38467.note: 0x9643 = 38467 = 10 × 3600 + 41 × 60 + 7: the seconds of the day. 17 bits in bits 80–88 and 90–97, low bit first.

a-format.name: Format
a-format.note: B: 100 bits per second, one frame per second.

a-modulation.name: Modulation
a-modulation.note: 1: a sine wave whose amplitude carries the pulses, large during a pulse and small after it. 0 is a DC level shift (pulse width), 2 is Manchester.

a-carrier.name: Carrier
a-carrier.note: 2: a 1 kHz carrier. 0 means no carrier, as with a DC level shift.

a-content.name: Content
a-content.note: 4: BCD time of year, year, control bits and straight binary seconds. 0 is the same without the year; 7 has no control bits.

facts.standard: IRIG Standard 200 (time codes); IEEE C37.118.1 for the meaning of the control bits
facts.between: GPS clock → relays, meters and recorders in the same building
facts.transport: Coax or twisted pair: DC level shift (B00x) or a 1 kHz sine (B12x)
facts.frames: One frame per second: 100 bits of 10 ms
facts.speed: A DC level shift keeps relays within about a microsecond; the modulated sine is less exact

tips: Agree whether the clock sends UTC or local time. In local time the offset bits say by how much, but IEEE 1344 and IEEE C37.118 read their sign the opposite way.
An input set for B00x (DC level) cannot read a B12x (1 kHz sine) output, and the other way round. Check the code at both ends.
One DC output drives a limited number of inputs. Add up the load of every relay on the line, and check the polarity of each pair.
Clocks name the same signal differently: what one calls B000 with IEEE 1344 on, another calls B004. Compare the bits, not the names.

timing.title: The first 110 ms of a frame
timing.note: The frame for 10:41:07 begins with two markers in a row: P0 ends the last frame, Pr starts this one, and the rising edge of Pr is exactly 10:41:07.000. Then the seconds, units first: 1, 1, 1, 0 = 7. B00x sends the pulses as DC levels: 2 ms for a 0, 5 ms for a 1, 8 ms for a marker. B12x puts the same pulses on a 1 kHz sine, loud during the pulse and quiet after it (about 10 to 3). The sine is drawn here as steps.
